After several hundred hours, I think this finally deserves a review.

Gladius is a 4X turn-based game with a rich lore and myriads of factions thanks to being based in the Warhammer 40,000 universe. The base game offers 4 factions, though there are 7 more faction DLCs. Notable, all factions feature different mechanics - from the Space Marine with only one big city, the ever-regenerating Necrons or the WAAAGH of the Orks. Unique for modern 4X, the game features no diplomacy - in my eyes, as a vivid fan of games like Advance Wars or Battle for Wesnoth, thats a big plus. There is only war after all!

The important thing is that even with each their own mechanics, each faction still feels accessible for someone willing to learn. Yes, not being able to expand as Space Marine may seem disadvantageous, but after learning the pros and cons of each faction you start to recognize the different strategies and builds for them. Enjoy a more hit-and-run style of gameplay? The Drukhari offer it with a focus on Assault transport units and teleportation. Want more ranged focus and customizable units? T´au it is. Want strong specialized cities which will make your late-game unstoppable? AdMech offers that. Of course, with neutral units patrolling and a randomly generated map, each game is different enough to challenge you.

Each faction offers a series of quests - which often spawn neutral units to defeat and enable you to win the game without killing all enemy factions (as reaching the end of the quest-line counts as winning immediately), though I tend to play without them (you can simply turn them off in the lobby options) since I like Gladius for its straightforward turn-based strategy character.

I´m split on the DLC-policy - its nice to have faction DLCs - if you don´t want to play a faction, you don´t have to get the DLC - you are not missing out on something for your faction. Thats a big plus, but the unit DLCs are not that great if you only enjoy a few factions - basically every unit DLC is in the format "one unit for each faction" with the latter even giving only some factions a unit. If you only want to play Orks for example, a unit DLC may include one new Ork unit - and 7 units for factions you don´t play. The only exception being the Ultima Founding DLC, which only gives the Space Marines more units - a step I would have liked for every faction.

Btw, someone new might look at the list of DLC and think "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, DLC for over 200€!" - wait for a discount. Both the game and older DLC (older = everything but the last one or two) are usually discounted for over 40%, the base game even up to 90% percent.

Using DLC in multiplayer is both good and bad. Each player can only choose the factions he personally owns - host has Tyranids, you not? Then only host can play Tyranids (and choose them for AI). But the unit DLCs only depend on what the host owns - in my friend group I usually host, so as long as I own the unit packs, everyone can use them and only has to get the faction DLCs.

Another good thing about the game is the modding community - from graphic mods to change the scale of unit sizes, to new units or even new factions, the game features a plethora of mod options. 

Well, I stated several bad and good things, whats my resumee? Gladius is a really good, 4X-game with a clear focus on eXterminate. The lack of diplomacy makes it clear from the beginning that you have to kill each enemy, and it hosts a multitude of both diverse factions and units, making each game feel different. If you are on the fence, wait for a discount - it gets as low as around 4€.

TLDR: I´d highly recommend it.

Yes, the pricing model is a little gross. Let's hit that first. The base game (free at time of writing) goes on sale for just $4 at least 20 times a year, but looking at the list and cost of DLC as a newcomer can be shocking. Even on sale, you could spend +$150, with many just adding a few units here and there.

My approach was not to "save" money by getting the big bundle, but instead to buy one faction at a time, learn it through a few games, then look through the list of unit packs and pick one that would add something to my fav factions. The game is pretty simple, but the factions have very unique play! Tyranids, for one, feel very "alien" to the rest of the cast, with their tile eating eco mechanic. I would look forward to the next faction, the next sale. If ever I got sick of the game, I'd not spend another dime, and the value I'd already spent would be paid back many times over in my playtime.

'Warhammer 40,000: Gladius - Relics of War' successfully translates the grimdark atmosphere of the 41st millennium into a focused, combat-oriented 4X strategy game. By stripping away the diplomatic layers typical of the genre and leaning into the "there is only war" mantra, it creates a streamlined experience where city-building and resource management exist solely to fuel a massive military machine. The faction asymmetry is a major highlight; playing as the Necrons feels fundamentally different from the Space Marines or Orks, with unique mechanics that stay faithful to the deep lore of the franchise. The tactical depth provided by terrain modifiers and unit leveling ensures that every skirmish on the surface of Gladius Prime feels impactful and rewarding.

However, the game’s singular focus on warfare can make the experience feel somewhat one-dimensional during extended play sessions. Without the political maneuvering or trade systems found in competitors like Civilization, the late-game can occasionally devolve into a repetitive grind of unit production and movement. Additionally, while the base game is solid, much of the faction variety is locked behind a extensive list of DLC, which can make the initial package feel incomplete for fans wanting the full tabletop roster.

Ultimately, 'Warhammer 40,000: Gladius - Relics of War' is a highly competent and atmospheric strategy title that perfectly captures the brutal essence of its setting, though its lack of non-military win conditions may limit its appeal for those seeking a more traditional, multi-faceted 4X experience.

This game just disappoints me so hard. It's managed to breathe fresh air into the often diplomacy or "tall-gameplay" focused games of its kind. It is set in the Warhammer universe to boot... Unfortunately, it fails so fundamentally as a single-player 4X experience, and crumbles under its own decisions down the line.

Gladius has iterated on what other "Civ-like" 4X games are already good at - the early game. It is filled with combat instead of relying on just city-building. The exploration interacts with the game's combat system that has a bunch of abilities, an actual damage/health system, morale, unit counts, and faction-specific diverse mechanics. It's certainly more advanced and heavily combat focused compared to other games like it.

However, the mid-late game still leaves a lot to be desired, and is perhaps worse than its competitors. The lack of diplomacy or any win-con other than conquest is instead replaced by boring faction quests that are detached from the game itself. Now, I love the idea that conquest is the only option as it fits the theme, but it isn't actually the case here. It's a hollow promise.

The fundamental issue as always is that the AI cheats. It's not actually an interesting opponent, and so if you make it to the late game you are faced with either a trivial slog of conquest, or faction-dependent questlines that spawn a bunch of neutral enemies in extreme ludo-narrative dissonance fashion (sorry I used that word). Believability suffers. It feels like a DND campaign hosted by GPT-3 that suddenly shouts "And then suddenly, God appeared!" The difficulty is extremely front-loaded or served in odd events that are disconnected from the game you are actually playing.

Seriously... Somehow they managed to shoehorn linear questlines into 4X games! You have no opportunity to come up with some intrinsic goal of your own, as your faction's questline is set in stone from the beginning. You can choose not to follow that, but as I mentioned interacting with the AI factions is either dead simple or an uninteresting slog...

Fundamentally, there are just not that many interesting possibilities other than experiencing a glimpse of your favorite 40k faction. That's cool and all, but I can just go and play the tabletop game which is infinitely more interesting and open-ended.

It's a bit of a shame, because the WH40K aesthetic is genuinely awesome and executed so well in this game. The factions don't just have aesthetic differences but vary a lot in their mechanics. They have gameplay identity. There are limitations on their expansion, combat, and exploration mechanics depending on their faction identity, and it's such a massive improvement over other games in this regard. Not to mention the music of the factions, and ofc the sounds and the unit VA (though non-DLC factions are a bit limited in this regard. MARINES HAVE NO SOUNDS LOLOLOL serves em right :P).

So yeah... They are able to pull of such different gameplay for the factions because fundamentally it doesn't matter. You'll just do a pre-designed questline and be sent on your way to try out the new DLC.

The fundamental issues with the game are just too big for me to enjoy it unfortunately. I am sure it could be a lot of fun in multiplayer, if you don't mind organizing a multiple-hours long campaign with friends or sitting through it in one big session in a random lobby. I did have a blast when I played with a friend, but it's a bit inconvenient to organize for a game of this length imo, so the single player should be good too. Almost any average 4X game has this issue for me...
